prācyaprameyeṇa saha asya prameyasya samuccayārthaḥ | aṃśatrayasamuccayastu ekenaiva cakāreṇa || 9 || atha yaduktam eko maheśvaraḥ iti, tatra aikyaṃ tāvat nigamayati sūtreṇa tadaikyena vinā na syātsaṃvidāṃ lokapaddhatiḥ | prakāśaikyāt tadekatvaṃ mātaikaḥ sa iti sthitam || 10 || tasmāduktarūpāt prameyāt hetoridaṃ jātam- yat kila saṃvidāṃ (page 433) jñānānāmaikyena vinā lokamārgaḥ sarvo vyavahāro na bhavet, asti ca ayaṃ, tasmādavaśyaṃ saṃvidāmaikyam | naca tat durupapādam | prakāśa eva hi saṃvidāṃ paramārthaḥ, sa ca eko bhedābhāvāt | yaśca asāvekaḥ, sa eva paramārthataḥ pramātā,- iti yadiha upadeśyaṃ, tadadhunā sthiraṃ niṣkampaṃ jātam | vṛttau paramātma ityanena paramārthapramātṛtāmasya āha | tathāhi ajaḍapramātṛsiddhiḥ yadyapyarthasthitiḥ............................ | (20) iti | ityādināca iti | ākārato bhavanmukhyo bhedaḥ, sa nāsti,-iti svarūpagrahaṇena uktam | tatraiva hetuḥ cinmātrarūpatvāt iti | deśakālābhyāmapi na bheda ityāha deśa iti | yadyapi vicitrabhedo vyavahāra uktaḥ, tathāpi vyāpakatvāt sarvasaṅgrāhī pratipādyapratipādakabhāva iha uktaḥ, sa hi svātmani api saṃśayavitarkanirṇayādau, paratra ca upadeśakrayavikrayādau saṃbhavatyeva, tena vinā hi vyavahārasya api avyavahāryatvam | nanu jñānānāṃ svasaṃvedane sve sve yojanālakṣaṇā viśrāntiriti kimetadapūrvamityāśaṅkāyāmāha yadica iti | saṃvedyātmanām iti saṃvedyasya nīlāderātmabhūtānām | nīlāderhi prakāśa eva paramārtho rūpam | anenaiva ca vāstavamaikyameva ucitamiti uktam | nanu evaṃ nīlādinā api kathamuparāgaḥ kriyate yena uktaṃ tattatsaṃvedyopahitānām iti | ucyate- māyāśaktyā kṛtabhedaḥ prakāśāt vyatirecita iva, tata eva bhinnaḥ, parasparato'pi vyatiricyamāno yaḥ saṃvedyalakṣaṇo bhāgaḥ prakāśasyaiva aṃśaḥ, tena tā bheditāstāsām | prakāśaḥ (page 434) iti sāṅkhyajaiminīyānāṃ svapakāśā saṃviditi sthitam | cirantanavaiśeṣikāṇāmapi citsvabhāva eva ātmeti uktaṃ jñānaṃ ca citsvarūpaṃ ca................... | (1|2|7) ityetatsūtravivṛtau | bauddhairapi buddheśca grāhikā bud
**The knowers are one, and the one is the Lord** The jñānādhikāra — the whole first adhikāra of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī — comes to its close. And it closes, fittingly, on the unity. It was said at the start that the one is the maheśvara; now the unity is established. Kārikā 10: without that unity, the world-path of the consciousnesses would not be; from the manifestation-unity, that one-ness, that one alone is the knower, it is established. The argument is simple and decisive. The whole dealing of the world — the path by which consciousnesses know, remember, and act together — would be impossible if the consciousnesses were a scattered crowd of mutually opaque streams. But the dealing is; so the consciousnesses must be one. And this is not hard to accept, for the manifestation (prakāśa) is the very essence of the consciousnesses, and the manifestation is one — there is no difference in the light itself. That one manifestation is, in truth, the knower. The one light that shines in all the consciousnesses is the one knower, the param-essence knower, the paramātman. Even the Sāṃkhya's and the Jaiminīya's self-luminous consciousness, and the ancient Vaiśeṣika's consciousness-nature self, all point to this one. The objection comes: "each cognition rests, in its own self-experience, in its own joining — what is new here?" And the answer is that the known itself — the blue and the rest — has the manifestation as its param-essence; the blue is, in its being, the light. So the unity is real, not a construction. And the apparent difference of the known is made only by the māyā-power: the known-marker part, made distinct from the manifestation as if it were other, is still the manifestation's own part. The difference is the māyā's making; the unity is the truth. And the Sāṃkhya's puruṣa — the separate self it posits — is not another at all. It is the un-recognized own-lordship, the contracted consciousness; its knowledge and action, dealt as "I," are the "I"-recollection. And this "I"-recollection, Abhinavagupta notes, is the pervader of all the states — the pure, the mixed, the un-pure — gathered, not abandoned. The threefold self-recognition runs through them all. Then kārikā 11 sums up the whole: he alone, by the fixed reflexive-awareness-ness, is the great Lord; the reflexive-awareness alone, of the God, in the pure knowledge-action, since. The great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive-awareness — the one who is aware of himself, fixedly, is the Lord; and that reflexive-awareness is the God's own pure knowledge-and-action. The great-Lordship is not an added power; it is the self-awareness itself, the "I" that knows and acts, the one knower. And so the jñānādhikāra — the adhikāra on knowledge — is complete. The ||8|| colophon closes the vimarśa on the great-Lordship in the one-support of the powers; and the great colophon reads: "completed — this, the first jñānādhikāra." The first of the four adhikāras of the IPVV is done. It has established the self, the powers, the one knower, the great-Lordship — all culminating in the unity: the one manifestation is the one knower, and the one knower, aware of himself, is the Lord. ---

> The passage closes the jñānādhikāra with the unity of the knowers. Kārikā 10: the whole dealing of > the world — the path by which consciousnesses know, remember, and act together — would be impossible > if the consciousnesses were mutually opaque streams; but the dealing is, so the consciousnesses must > be one. The unity is argued via the dealing, not by a bare assertion of identity. The Sāṃkhya's > separate puruṣa is then re-read: it is not another self but the un-recognized own-lordship, the > contracted consciousness. > > Kārikā 11 draws the conclusion: the great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive awareness. The > Lordship is not a fifth power added to the four; it is what the four are. The powers reduce to the > self-awareness, and the self-awareness is the Lord. > > The passage argues the unity via the dealing and identifies the Lordship with the self-awareness. It > does not by itself establish the identity of all supports by the felt alone; that is a further claim.
